issues.legal_issue: A plaintiff seeking relief for alleged encroachment must prove that the disputed land forms part of the property claimed by the plaintiff.
material_facts: The plaintiffs sought injunctions and removal of structures on land they claimed had been encroached upon.
The plaintiffs relied on a document allocating different land identifiers to the respective plots, but the disputed land’s identity as part of their plots was not established by that document alone.
The courts below placed a burden on the defendants to establish their position concerning the land.
issues.conclusion: The burden was on the plaintiffs to prove that the disputed land formed part of the properties they claimed; the suit could not be decreed on the document alone.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 101 of the Indian Evidence Act, the party asserting a fact necessary to obtain judgment bears the burden of proving it. Section 83 did not assist in establishing the disputed land’s identity in this case. A record of rights is not a document of title. In Narain Prasad Aggarwal (D) by LRs. v. State of M.P. [2007 (8) SCALE 250], the Court held that entries in a record of rights are admissible and may carry a rebuttable presumption of correctness, but do not constitute title.

predicates.injunction_suit: A plaintiff brought a suit seeking injunctive relief concerning land.
predicates.plaintiff_claims_encroachment: The plaintiff alleged that another party had encroached on land claimed by the plaintiff.
predicates.land_identity_disputed: The parties disputed whether the land at issue formed part of the property claimed by the plaintiff.

issues.definition: When an injunction suit concerns alleged encroachment on land whose identity is disputed, the plaintiff must prove that the land is part of the property claimed.

issues.legal_issue: Revenue records may support a rebuttable inference of possession but do not establish title to property.
material_facts: The courts below considered revenue-record entries and a document identifying land parcels in deciding the property dispute.
A revenue-record entry showed the Municipal Corporation’s name in respect of the land adjoining the disputed plots.
The trial court nevertheless proceeded on the basis that the adjoining property might belong to the defendants.
issues.conclusion: The courts were required to assess the records under the correct principles: revenue records are not documents of title, though they may be relevant to possession and carry a rebuttable presumption.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 35 of the Indian Evidence Act, entries in a record of rights are admissible as relevant evidence and may carry a rebuttable presumption of correctness, but they are not documents of title. A revenue record raises a presumption regarding possession, and Section 110 of the Act may support presumptions of possession and its continuity. The Court relied on Narain Prasad Aggarwal (D) by LRs. v. State of M.P. [2007 (8) SCALE 250] concerning the evidentiary status of record-of-rights entries.

predicates.property_rights_dispute: The parties disputed rights in identified property.
predicates.revenue_records_relied_on: A party or court relied on entries in revenue records concerning the property.

issues.definition: In a property-rights dispute where revenue records are relied on, those records support only a rebuttable inference about possession and do not establish title.

issues.legal_issue: A court cannot grant permanent mandatory relief while leaving the underlying title dispute unresolved.
material_facts: The plaintiffs sought demolition of structures and other mandatory relief, as well as an injunction.
The courts granted mandatory relief although the plaintiffs had not sought a declaration of title and the courts left the title question open.
The High Court considered that the defendants could pursue their title remedies later, although demolition could affect their ability to do so.
issues.conclusion: The courts could not grant a decree for permanent mandatory injunction while leaving the question of title undecided.
issues.legal_principle: The Court distinguished an interlocutory mandatory order made under Section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure to restore parties to the position they would have occupied had an injunction not been breached from a final decree granting permanent mandatory relief. The latter cannot be granted while leaving unresolved the title question on which the relief depends.

predicates.permanent_injunction_proceeding: A party brought a proceeding seeking permanent injunctive relief concerning property.
predicates.mandatory_demolition_relief_sought: The plaintiff asked the court to order the removal or demolition of structures.
predicates.title_left_unresolved: The court left undecided which party held title to the land affected by the requested relief.

issues.definition: When permanent injunctive proceedings seek demolition and title is left unresolved, final mandatory relief requires the title dispute to be decided.

issues.legal_issue: A commissioner’s report cannot be considered when the commissioner could not be cross-examined.
material_facts: An Advocate-Commissioner was appointed and filed a report in the suit.
An objection to the report was filed, and the commissioner could not be cross-examined.
The report formed part of the record.
issues.conclusion: The report could not be taken into consideration despite forming part of the record.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that the commissioner’s report could not be considered where the commissioner could not be cross-examined.

predicates.civil_property_suit: A party brought a civil suit concerning property.
predicates.commissioner_report_filed: A commissioner appointed in the suit submitted a report.
predicates.commissioner_not_cross_examined: The commissioner was not available to be cross-examined about the report.

issues.definition: In a civil property suit, a filed commissioner’s report cannot be considered when the commissioner was not cross-examined.

issues.legal_issue: A decree must be set aside and the matter reconsidered when the courts misallocate the burden of proof and grant mandatory relief without resolving the disputed land identity and title.
material_facts: The plaintiffs’ claim depended on proving that the disputed land formed part of their plots.
The courts below placed the burden of proof on the defendants and relied on evidence that did not establish the disputed land’s identity.
The courts granted mandatory relief while leaving title unresolved.
The Supreme Court considered that the parties should be able to adduce additional evidence and that a commissioner could be appointed to measure the land.
issues.conclusion: The impugned judgments were set aside and the matter was remitted to the trial court for fresh consideration, with liberty to seek amendment of the plaint and adduce additional evidence.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied Section 101 of the Indian Evidence Act and the principles governing proof of land identity, the evidentiary effect of revenue records, and permanent mandatory relief where title is unresolved. It remitted the matter for fresh consideration and permitted additional evidence and measurement by a commissioner.

rule.if: civil_property_suit and burden_shifted_to_defendants and land_identity_unproven and mandatory_decree_granted_with_title_unresolved

predicates.civil_property_suit: A party brought a civil suit concerning disputed property.
predicates.burden_shifted_to_defendants: The court placed on the defendants the burden of proving a matter necessary to the plaintiffs’ property claim.
predicates.land_identity_unproven: The evidence did not establish that the disputed land formed part of the property claimed by the plaintiffs.
predicates.mandatory_decree_granted_with_title_unre: The court ordered mandatory relief affecting the land while leaving title undecided.

issues.definition: When a civil property suit involves a shifted burden, unproven land identity, and mandatory relief granted without deciding title, the judgment is set aside and the matter is remanded.
